Rate My Tennis

Tennis Technique Report

In three minutes at the wall you hit about 70 balls: forehands, two-handed backhands and a few serves. A steady rhythm, eyes on the ball and a full turn on the forehand are a solid base. What holds you back most is bowing at the waist instead of bending the knees on low balls, a serve contact that is low and out to the side, and a forehand finish that stops too low. Fix those three first.

What you already do well

Backhand contact in front, both arms long

At contact the ball is ahead of your front foot, both arms are nearly straight and your head is still. This is the most important part of a two-handed backhand and you already have it.

Forehand turn and non-hitting arm

During the take-back your right hand reaches across toward the ball and your shoulders turn side-on, which leaves room to accelerate.

A relaxed, extended forehand when the spacing is right

On this swing you are the right distance from the ball: the arm is naturally long and the racket goes through the ball. Getting to this distance every time is the next goal.

Top things to fix

Fix firstForehand / backhand

1Bowing at the waist on low balls

Trunk lean at contact on low ballsNow 25–33°→Target 15° or less (get down with the knees)
What we see
When the ball is below your waist your knees hardly bend; you bow and drop the racket head to reach it. In this frame the trunk leans about 30° and both legs are close to straight.
Why it matters
Bowing drops your head and eyes with it, puts your weight on your toes and lets the racket head hang, so low balls go into the net or fly long. Straight legs also means no power from the legs.
How to fix it
Swap the bow for a sit: keep your back tall and bend your knees as if sitting on a bar stool, so your hips go down and the handle reaches ball height. Then push up through the shot.
CueSit, don't bow.
Drills
  • Wall-sit shadow swings — Back against a wall, thighs at about 45°, back flat. Make ten slow forehand and backhand swings and feel knees bent, back straight.3 sets of 10, daily
  • Low-ball feeds — Hit softly so the ball comes back low. On every shot the handle must be below your knees with your back upright; if not, stop the ball and start again.5 minutes each session
Fix firstServe

2Serve contact is low and out to the side

Hand height at contactNow just above the head, arm about 45° off vertical→Target arm close to vertical, fully extended
What we see
At contact your hitting arm reaches out to the side (about 45° from vertical) and the ball is only a little above your head. You do bend your knees before the hit, which is good.
Why it matters
Every 10 cm of contact height you give up shrinks the window over the net. A sideways swing is more of a sling: hard to hit down into the box, and harder on the shoulder.
How to fix it
Toss higher (a little above your fully raised racket) and closer to above your head, slightly in front. Then reach up and meet the ball at the top, with the arm nearly vertical and fully extended.
CueToss higher, reach up.
Drills
  • Kneeling serves — Serve with your back knee on the ground. The ball only clears the net if you reach to full height and hit up.15 balls each session
  • Toss to a target — Toss only: hold the racket up at full reach and freeze. The ball should peak at racket-head height and land about a foot in front of you.20 tosses daily
  • Touch the mark — Find a mark on a wall or fence that your fully raised racket just reaches. Touch it before each serve, then hit the ball at that height.10 balls each session
ImportantForehand

3Forehand finish is too low, with little low-to-high

Hand height at the finishNow between waist and chest→Target above the opposite shoulder
What we see
After most forehands the racket stops at waist or chest height; the swing travels almost level, like a push.
Why it matters
A low-to-high path is what puts topspin on the ball. Topspin lets you clear the net higher and still bring the ball down in the court, so the same effort gives far more margin.
How to fix it
Let the racket head drop below the ball first, then keep swinging forward and up until the back of your hand is by your right shoulder (left-hander finishing to the right), elbow pointing forward.
CueFinish with the racket on your right shoulder.
Drills
  • Touch-the-shoulder finish — After every forehand, freeze and check: hand by the right shoulder, elbow pointing forward. Twenty shadow swings first, then against the wall.20 shadow swings before each session
  • Over the line — Mark a line 1.5 m up the wall. Every forehand must clear it and come down with topspin.3 sets of 10 in a row
ImportantForehand

4Sometimes too close to the ball on the forehand

Elbow angle at contact (swing to swing)Now 84°–146°→Target steady, around 130–160°
What we see
On some balls the ball is already beside you, so you hit with the upper arm pinned and the elbow tightly bent. On others the spacing is right and the arm is long. The two alternate.
Why it matters
A cramped arm shortens the swing and makes the racket face hard to control, so both power and direction vary. Consistent spacing is the first source of consistency.
How to fix it
Start adjusting with small steps the moment the ball leaves the wall. Aim to meet it an arm plus a racket away, to the side and in front. When in doubt, take half a step back.
CueFeet first, give the arm room.
Drills
  • Split step — Make a small hop every time the ball hits the wall, then adjust your feet as you land.Throughout every session
  • Measure with a straight arm — No swing, just positioning: catch the ball on the strings with a straight arm so it meets the middle of the racket.20 balls
PolishTwo-handed backhand

5Late take-back on the two-handed backhand

Racket back to contactNow 0.13–0.23 s→Target 0.4 s or more
What we see
On several balls the ball has already bounced toward you when the racket is only just getting back, and then it has to come forward straight away.
Why it matters
A late take-back turns the swing into a rush: you can only muscle it with the arms, and contact drifts back.
How to fix it
The moment you read the ball to your backhand side, turn your shoulders with both hands on the racket. The turn is the take-back; you don't need a separate pull.
CueBall leaves the wall, shoulders are turned.
Drills
  • Turn-bounce-hit — Say "turn" when the ball hits the wall (your shoulder turn must be done by then), "bounce" when it lands, "hit" at contact.2 sets of 20

Training plan

Weeks 1–2

Get lower

  • Wall-sit shadow swings, 3 sets daily
  • 5 minutes of low balls at the wall: back tall, knees bent
  • Split step on every ball
Weeks 3–4

Serve contact point

  • 20 target tosses a day
  • 15 kneeling serves and 10 touch-the-mark serves
  • Film your serve from the side and check the contact height
Weeks 5–6

Topspin forehand finish

  • 20 touch-the-shoulder shadow swings
  • Over the 1.5 m line: 10 in a row
  • Record again from the same angle and compare with this report
